title: Pick One Sport and Its Paper
bigQuestion: What can the written papers of one sport tell us about who made its rules and who was kept out?

story.title: A Stack on the Library Desk
story.kicker: One student lays out one sport's founding papers in order and sees a pattern.
paragraphs: It is a gray afternoon at a public library in Chicago. A senior named Dana sits at a long table with a stack of photocopies. Every page comes from one sport: baseball. She has sorted them by year, oldest on top. A librarian has helped her find each one in books of reprinted documents and in online archives.

The top page is a short list of rules from the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York, dated 1845. Under it lies a report from the National Association of Base Ball Players, dated December 1867. Next comes the constitution of the National League, written in 1876 by club owners who met at a hotel in New York. A Chicago man, William Hulbert, led that meeting.

Farther down the stack is a paper from February 1920. It records the founding of the Negro National League at a YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. Rube Foster, owner of the Chicago American Giants, called that meeting. Near the bottom sits a news release from December 2020. In it, Major League Baseball says it now counts seven Negro Leagues as major leagues.

Dana reads the 1867 report twice. It says the national association should turn away any club with Black members. She checks the 1876 constitution. It says nothing about race at all. Yet no Black player appeared in the National League for decades. She writes a note in her margin: some lines are written down, and some are kept without being written.

By closing time, Dana has a timeline taped across two pages. Each date has a name beside it: a club, a league, a committee or a company. She can now say who wrote each rule, when, and who it left out. Her stack of paper has become the start of a history.
story.think: Why might a rule that was never written down be harder to prove than one that was?

lessons.title: Two Kinds of Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Most sports bodies keep two kinds of paper: a constitution that sets up the body and a rule book that sets out the game.
reading: On 26 October 1863, men from about a dozen London clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern on Great Queen Street. They formed the Football Association, or FA. Ebenezer Cobb Morley, a lawyer, served as its first secretary. The meeting set up the body first: its name, its members and how it would vote.

Over the next six weeks, the members argued about the game itself. On 8 December 1863, they adopted thirteen written Laws of the Game. The Laws banned carrying the ball in the hands and banned hacking, which meant kicking an opponent's shins. The Blackheath club disagreed and left. In 1871, clubs that wanted handling formed the Rugby Football Union.

The FA's story shows two different kinds of paper. A *constitution* sets up a body: who may join, who leads, how votes are counted and how money is handled. The *bylaws* of a body add detailed rules for running the body's meetings. A *rule book* is different. It sets out how the game is scored, how long it lasts and what is allowed on the field.

A historian studying one sport needs both. The constitution tells who held power. The rule book tells what that power produced. A change in either one leaves a date on paper, and each date can be checked. London sporting newspapers reported the 1863 meetings, giving historians a second record to check against the FA's own.

words.d: the founding document of a body; it says who may join, who leads and how decisions are made
detailed rules for running a body's meetings, officers and money
the written rules of the game itself: scoring, time and what is allowed
the governing body of football in England, founded in London on 26 October 1863

lessons.title: A League Written in 1876
lessons.mainIdea: The 1876 National League constitution put club owners, not players, in charge of professional baseball.
reading: On 2 February 1876, representatives of eight baseball clubs met at the Grand Central Hotel in New York City. William Hulbert, an officer of the Chicago White Stockings, had called them together. They formed the National League of Professional Base Ball Clubs. Morgan Bulkeley of Hartford became its first president, and Hulbert soon followed him.

The older National Association of Professional Base Ball Players, founded in 1871, had been run largely by players. Clubs came and went, and many games were thought to be fixed by gamblers. The new league's constitution made the *club*, not the player, the member. Owners held the votes. Each member club had to come from a city of at least 75,000 people.

The constitution also banned gambling by players and club officers. In 1877, the league expelled four Louisville players for throwing games. Later rules barred Sunday games and the sale of alcohol at league parks. When Cincinnati sold beer and rented its grounds on Sundays, the league pushed it out after the 1880 season.

The document shaped what came next. In 1882, a rival called the American Association formed. It sold beer and charged 25 cents a ticket, half the National League's usual 50 cents. The two leagues show how a *charter*, a founding paper that grants a group its powers, can decide who can afford a seat as well as who can play.

words.d: in early professional baseball, the business that owned a team and held a vote in the league
a founding paper that creates a group and grants it powers
the professional baseball league founded in New York on 2 February 1876
to force a member out of a group by a vote

check.why: The National League made clubs, run by owners, its voting members.

check.why: Cincinnati broke league rules by selling beer and renting its park on Sundays.

lessons.title: Rules Put Into Print
lessons.mainIdea: Many modern sports can be dated from the year their rules were first written down and printed.
reading: Before printing, most games followed local custom. Each village, school or club played its own way. When teams from different places met, they first had to agree on rules. Writing the rules down made it possible for strangers to play the same game. In England, public schools such as Eton, Harrow and Rugby each kept their own football rules.

In New York, the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club wrote down a list of twenty rules in September 1845. In London, the FA printed its Laws in December 1863. In 1867, a Welsh sportsman named John Graham Chambers wrote a set of boxing rules. They were published under the name of the Marquess of Queensberry, who supported them. These are called the *Queensberry Rules*.

In December 1891, James Naismith wrote thirteen rules for a new game at the YMCA International Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. On 15 January 1892, the school's newspaper, *The Triangle*, printed them. YMCA branches across the country read that paper. Within a few years, basketball was being played far from Springfield.

A printed rule is a *primary source*: a record made at the time by the people involved. A later story about the rules is a *secondary source*. Historians trust a printed date more than a memory, because the paper can be seen and checked. A modern textbook chapter about Naismith's rules is a secondary source.

words.d: boxing rules written by John Graham Chambers and published in 1867 under the Marquess of Queensberry's name
the newspaper of the YMCA training school in Springfield, which printed Naismith's basketball rules in January 1892
a record made at the time by people who were there, such as a printed rule book or meeting minutes
a later account written by someone studying the past

check.why: The Triangle, the Springfield YMCA school's paper, printed the rules on 15 January 1892.

check.q: Which is a primary source about early basketball?
check.why: The rules printed in 1892 were made at the time by the people involved.

lessons.title: Who May Change a Law
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886, only the International Football Association Board can change soccer's Laws of the Game.
reading: England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland had each set up a separate football association by the 1880s. Their rules did not fully match. When their teams met, arguments followed. On 2 June 1886, the four associations held the first meeting of the *International Football Association Board*, or IFAB, in London.

The IFAB became the only body that could change the Laws. A change needed a large majority of votes. This made the Laws slow to change and hard for one country to control. FIFA, founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 by seven European associations, joined the IFAB in 1913.

Today the IFAB has four British votes and four FIFA votes. A change needs six of the eight. That rule means neither side can change the game alone. The IFAB meets each year at its *annual general meeting*, and new Laws usually take effect on 1 July. FIFA's four votes speak for all of its member nations together.

For a historian, this structure is useful. Every change to soccer's Laws has a meeting, a year and a body attached to it. A student can trace when a rule appeared by reading the IFAB's yearly editions of the Laws of the Game. The Laws have been revised many times; a major rewrite in 2016 made the text shorter and clearer.

words.d: IFAB; the body, formed in 1886, that alone can change soccer's Laws of the Game
the world governing body of soccer, founded in Paris in 1904
a yearly meeting where a body's members vote on changes
more than half of the votes; some bodies require a larger share for big changes

look.title: Eight Seats at One Table
look.text: Picture a meeting room. Four seats belong to the football associations of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Four belong to FIFA, which speaks for more than two hundred national associations. A proposal to change a Law needs six votes to pass.
look.prompt: Why might the four British associations still hold half the votes? What does that tell you about where the Laws were first written?

check.why: The four British associations held the IFAB's first meeting in London on 2 June 1886.

check.why: A change needs six of eight votes, so neither the British side nor FIFA can act alone.

check.why: Seven European associations founded FIFA in Paris on 21 May 1904.

lessons.title: A Crisis Writes New Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Deaths and injuries in college football in 1905 led to a new national body in 1906, which became the NCAA.
reading: College football in 1905 was rough and often deadly. Newspapers counted about eighteen deaths that season, many of them among young players. Columbia was among the colleges that gave up football. Others threatened to. In October 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt invited coaches and officials from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House to discuss the game.

After a player died in a game between Union College and New York University that November, NYU chancellor Henry MacCracken called a meeting of colleges. On 31 March 1906, sixty-two schools founded the *Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States*, or IAAUS. In 1910, it took a new name: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or *NCAA*.

The 1906 rules committee made changes that are still named in histories of the game. It legalized the forward pass and raised the distance needed for a first down from five yards to ten. These rules were meant to open up play and reduce the crushing mass of bodies in the middle of the field.

The paper trail here is rich. There are newspaper death counts, White House records, meeting minutes and the rule books of 1906. Together they show how public pressure produced a new *governing body* and new written rules in less than a year. At first the IAAUS mainly made rules. Its first national championship, in track and field, came in 1921.

words.w: Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States
words.d: IAAUS; the body of 62 colleges founded on 31 March 1906; renamed the NCAA in 1910
National Collegiate Athletic Association; the governing body for many U.S. college sports
an organization with the power to set rules and run competitions for a sport
a group chosen by a governing body to write and change the rules of the game

choices: Games were limited to college seniors.
check.why: The forward pass became legal under the 1906 college rules.

lessons.title: Rules for High Schools
lessons.mainIdea: State associations like the IHSA, founded in 1900, and a national federation formed in Chicago in 1920 wrote rules for high school sport.
reading: In the late 1800s, high school teams were often run by students. Some teams used older players who were not enrolled. Principals worried about fairness and schoolwork. In Illinois, principals formed a state body in 1900. Today it is called the Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*.

The IHSA wrote *eligibility* rules. These decide who may play: a player had to be a student, passing classes and under an age limit. The IHSA also ran state tournaments. Its first boys' tennis state champion was crowned in 1912. Its boys' wrestling state series began in 1937.

State associations soon wanted to work together. On 14 May 1920, L. W. Smith, the secretary of the Illinois association, hosted a meeting in Chicago. Representatives came from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin. They formed the group that became the *National Federation of State High School Associations*, or NFHS.

Over time, the NFHS began writing its own rule books for high school sports. Today it publishes rule books for many sports, used by high schools across the country. A student studying one sport can compare the NFHS rules with the NCAA's college rules and a pro league's rules. The three rule books often differ, and each difference has a date.

words.d: Illinois High School Association; the body founded in 1900 that runs high school sport in Illinois
the rules that decide who may take part in a sport

words.w: National Federation of State High School Associations
words.d: NFHS; the national group of state school associations, begun at a Chicago meeting in 1920
a set of tournaments run by a state association that ends in a state championship

lessons.title: The December 1867 Report
lessons.mainIdea: In 1867, a committee of the national baseball association wrote that clubs with Black members should be turned away.
reading: The National Association of Base Ball Players held its first convention in New York in 1857. It began with clubs from the New York area. By 1867 its member clubs came from many states, including Pennsylvania. Each year, a *nominating committee* reviewed which clubs could join.

The Pythian Base Ball Club of Philadelphia was a Black club led by Octavius Catto, a teacher and civil rights leader. In October 1867, the Pythians applied to the Pennsylvania state baseball association. Their delegate learned they would be voted down and withdrew the application.

At the national convention in December 1867, the nominating committee issued its report. It said the association should not admit any club that had one or more Black members. The committee wrote that it hoped to keep politics out of the association. The report put the exclusion into the association's official record.

Catto kept fighting for equal rights in Philadelphia. On 10 October 1871, election day, he was shot and killed on a Philadelphia street. The 1867 report is a primary source that historians use to date the first written *color line* in organized baseball.

words.d: a small group that reviews who may join a body and reports to the full membership
a rule or practice that kept Black people out of teams, leagues or places
a Black baseball club in Philadelphia led by Octavius Catto after the Civil War
a large meeting of a body's members to vote on its business

look.text: The committee recommends that no club with one or more colored persons be admitted. It says this is to keep out of the association any question that might cause division.
look.cite: Report of the Nominating Committee, National Association of Base Ball Players, annual convention, December 1867
look.prompt: What reason did the committee give for the exclusion? What does that reason leave unsaid?

check.why: Octavius Catto, a teacher and civil rights leader, led the Pythians.

choices: that clubs with Black members not be admitted

lessons.title: Lines Nobody Signed
lessons.mainIdea: Most of professional sport's color lines were unwritten agreements, so their start and end are dated by who played, not by a rule.
reading: In 1884, Moses Fleetwood Walker caught for the Toledo Blue Stockings of the American Association, then a major league. His brother Weldy also played a few games. In July 1887, the directors of the minor International League voted to approve no new contracts with Black players. After that, Black players were pushed out of white professional baseball.

No major league ever printed a rule against Black players. Owners simply did not sign them. Historians call this kind of exclusion an *unwritten rule* or a *gentlemen's agreement*. Because it was never written, its end is dated by a player's first game, not by a vote.

Black players built their own institutions. On 13 February 1920, Rube Foster and other owners met at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. They founded the *Negro National League*. Foster owned and managed the Chicago American Giants. Other Negro leagues followed in the 1920s and 1930s.

Jackie Robinson played his first game for the Brooklyn Dodgers on 15 April 1947. In other leagues, the dates differ. Kenny Washington and Woody Strode joined the Los Angeles Rams in 1946. Earl Lloyd played in the NBA in 1950, and Willie O'Ree skated for the Boston Bruins in 1958.

words.d: a practice everyone in a group follows even though it appears in no document
an unwritten understanding among powerful people, such as owners agreeing not to sign Black players
the Black baseball league founded by Rube Foster and other owners in Kansas City on 13 February 1920
opening a team, league or place to people who were kept out, especially by race

choices: to approve no new contracts with Black players
check.why: The directors voted to approve no new contracts with Black players, helping push them out.

check.q: Where was the Negro National League founded in 1920?
choices: at a hotel in New York
at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City

check.q: Why is the end of the major league color line dated by Jackie Robinson's first game?

check.why: The color line was an unwritten agreement, so its end is dated by who played, not by a vote.

lessons.title: A Ban on Women's Football
lessons.mainIdea: On 5 December 1921, the FA banned women's football from its members' grounds, and the ban lasted fifty years.
reading: During the First World War, women worked in British factories that made weapons and supplies. Many factories formed women's football teams. The best known came from the Dick, Kerr and Company works in Preston. On Boxing Day 1920, the *Dick, Kerr Ladies* drew about 53,000 people to Goodison Park in Liverpool.

Women's matches often raised money for charity and for wounded soldiers. On 5 December 1921, the FA council passed a resolution. It said football was unsuitable for women and should not be encouraged. It asked its member clubs not to let women's teams use their grounds.

The ban did not forbid women from playing. It closed the large stadiums, the paid officials and the crowds. Women's teams had to play on rougher public fields. The *resolution* stayed in force for fifty years. Some teams kept touring. In 1922 the Dick, Kerr Ladies traveled to the United States and played men's teams there.

In 1969, the Women's Football Association formed in England. The FA lifted its ban in 1971. The paper trail runs from the council's minutes of 1921 to the vote of 1971. Both dates are in the FA's own records, which makes this exclusion easy to cite. In 2022, England's women won the European Championship at Wembley Stadium.

words.d: a formal decision voted on and recorded by a body's council or members
a women's football team from a factory in Preston, England, that drew huge crowds around 1920
the group of elected leaders who make decisions for a governing body
an official order that forbids something

look.title: The FA Council, December 1921

look.cite: Football Association, resolution of the council, 5 December 1921
look.prompt: The resolution did not tell women to stop playing. How could it still shut them out?

check.why: About 53,000 people came to Goodison Park to watch them.

check.q: What did the FA's 1921 resolution do?

It asked member clubs not to let women's teams use their grounds.

check.why: The resolution closed members' grounds to women's teams; it did not make playing illegal.

check.q: When did the FA lift its ban on women's football?
check.why: The Women's Football Association formed in 1969, and the FA lifted the ban in 1971.

lessons.title: Memory Versus Minutes
lessons.mainIdea: Records made at the time are stronger evidence than stories told decades later, and some famous origin stories are legends.
reading: In 1905, the sporting goods maker Albert Spalding set up a panel to decide where baseball came from. It was led by Abraham G. Mills, a former National League president, and is known as the *Mills Commission*. Spalding wanted baseball to be seen as purely American, not as a child of the English game rounders.

The commission's report, dated 30 December 1907, named Abner Doubleday as the inventor of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. Its main evidence was a letter from a mining engineer named Abner Graves, who recalled events from his boyhood. Doubleday was a cadet at West Point in 1839. He never claimed to have invented baseball. Historians treat the Doubleday story as a *legend*.

Naismith's case is different. His rules were printed in January 1892, weeks after the first game. Almost fifty years later, he wrote a book, Basketball: Its Origin and Development, published in 1941 after his death in 1939. The book is a *memoir*, a personal account written from memory.

Historians use both kinds of papers but weigh them differently. The 1892 print is strong evidence about the first rules. The 1941 memoir tells what Naismith remembered and believed. When a memory and a record disagree, the record made at the time usually wins.

words.d: a panel set up in 1905 that in 1907 wrongly named Abner Doubleday as the inventor of baseball
a traditional story told as history that records do not support
a personal account of past events written from the writer's own memory
to support a claim with a second, independent piece of evidence

lessons.title: Naming the Body and the Year
lessons.mainIdea: A good citation of a sports document names the body that issued it, the document's title and its year or edition.
reading: Rule books change often, so the year matters. The IFAB publishes a new edition of the Laws of the Game each year. Major League Baseball publishes the Official Baseball Rules with a year on the cover. A rule quoted from the 1950 edition may not be in the 2020 edition. A *citation* must say which one.

Laws have dates too. President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972 on 23 June 1972. *Title IX* is one section of that law. It bars sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money. The government's detailed regulations explaining how Title IX applied to school sports came later, in 1975.

The body matters as much as the date. Different bodies govern different levels of the same sport. A high school game in Illinois follows rules adopted by the IHSA and the NFHS. A college game follows NCAA rules. A professional game follows the league's own book. Naming the *issuing body* tells a reader whose power stood behind a rule.

Put together, a strong citation reads like this: body, title, year. For example: Football Association, council resolution, 5 December 1921. Or: National Association of Base Ball Players, nominating committee report, December 1867. Or: Education Amendments of 1972, Title IX, signed 23 June 1972.

words.d: a short note naming where a fact came from so a reader can check it
one printing of a document in a given year; rule books have a new edition when rules change
the section of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bars sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
the organization that wrote or approved a document
a detailed rule written by a government agency to explain how a law works
